newsitem.title: NORWAY: Oil-rich Norway's economy continues to be strong.
newsitem.headline: Oil-rich Norway's economy continues to be strong.

text.p: Oil-rich Norway's economy is steaming ahead but inflation is forecast to be slightly higher in 1997 than this year because of soaring electricity prices, Statistics Norway said on Thursday.

The statistics office, in a quarterly report on key economic indicators, upgraded the annual 1997 inflation forecast to 2.2 percent from 2.0 percent in a similar forecast in June. The forecast for this year's growth was unchanged at 1.4 percent.

"Price growth in 1997 was revised upwards slightly because of the special circumstances on the power market, which we expect to be normalised again in 1998 and contribute to a lower inflation rate again," an economic outlook said.

Lack of snow and rain has driven up electricity prices to record highs in Norway, which relies almost exclusively on hydro power for energy. The country, which pumps 3.2 million barrels of oil per day, is the world's second largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia because it keeps only 150,000 barrels for domestic use.

"Norway has one of strongest economies in Euyope," a senior financial analyst said. "Norway is one of the few countries to fully comply with convergence criteria under the Maastricht treaty for European monetary union."
Ironically, Norway is not a member of the European Union.

The forecast kept the country's overall 1996 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth unchanged at 4.3 percent from the previous quarterly report, but upgraded 1997 GDP growth to 2.3 percent from 2.2 percent.
Mainland GDP growth, which excludes the thriving North Sea oil and gas sector, was kept unchanged at 3.0 percent for this year, but was raised by 0.1 percentage point to 2.4 percent for next year.
Meanwhile, overall GDP grew 0.3 percent in the second quarter of 1996 after rising 1.6 percent in the first quarter.

The statistics office said strong export growth and unexpectedly high oil prices would lead to a major increase in the current account surplus. First-half current account surplus stood at 34.3 billion crowns compared with 16.1 billion in the first half of last year.
"If we removed the oil income we would have a deficit in the current account," the analyst said.
The statistics office upgraded its forecast for the current account surplus for the whole of 1996 to 52 billion crowns from a projected annual 44 billion crowns three months ago.
The outlook kept unemployment unchanged at 4.5 percent of the work force this year but put it at 4.2 percent next year, down 0.1 percentage point from June's forecast.

The finance ministry, which will issue a draft 1997 state budget in October, forecast a 1996 state budget surplus of 24.9 billion crowns in May, but experts expect the figure to be much higher because of the rising oil prices.
